segments.text: In the next eight minutes, I'll explain why you stay up when you're exhausted, and hand you three fixes for tonight.
But first, a question. You're tired. You know you're tired. So why does eleven PM feel like the best part of your day?
Here's the secret. It isn't that you hate sleep.
You've been borrowing from tomorrow Bob.
He's the guy you hand every problem to. Groggy, grumpy, and never once consulted.
He is not a fan.
First, this has an actual name. And it's less dramatic than you'd hope.
It's called bedtime procrastination. Researchers define it as going to bed later than you meant to, with no outside reason forcing you.
Kroese and colleagues wrote about it in two thousand fourteen. The "no outside reason" part is the key.
No deadline. No newborn. No night shift. Just you, a phone, and a very flexible idea of "ten more minutes."
That's what makes it odd. Nothing is actually stopping you from going to bed.
Except the part of you that doesn't want to.
So it's not a character flaw. It's a pattern, and patterns have causes.
Honest caveat. Not every late night is this. Shift work, young kids, and sleep problems are different stories.
Now let's talk about why your evening suddenly feels like the only time that belongs to you.
Think about your day. Work owns the morning. Chores own the afternoon. People who need things own the evening.
By ten PM, you finally have a few hours with nobody asking for anything. It feels like unclaimed land.
So you plant a flag. "This hour is mine." Nobody may touch it. Not even sleep.
Online, people nicknamed this revenge bedtime procrastination. It's an informal internet nickname, not a medical term.
Also, "revenge" is a bit dramatic. Against whom? Your alarm clock?
The feeling underneath is real, though. You want some time that isn't owed to anyone.
The catch is the price. You pay with sleep, and tomorrow Bob gets the bill.
Interest rate: one extremely grumpy morning.
But why can't you just stop? That's a brain problem. Let's go there.
Here's the cruel part. By night, self-control tends to run low. Researchers argue about exactly how that works, but you've felt it.
It's like a phone battery. At noon, full. At midnight, it's at one percent, and you're opening a game.
The same brain that said no to dessert at lunch now says yes to everything.
And then there's timing.
Scrolling pays off right now. Sleep pays off tomorrow.
People tend to favor rewards that come sooner. It's a very common tendency, and bedtime keeps losing to it.
So the vote is tonight Bob, all of them. Tomorrow Bob, none.
He wasn't invited.
It's not that you can't do math. It's that tomorrow feels like a stranger.
And a feed knows exactly what to do with a tired brain.
Now put that tired brain in front of a feed with no bottom. No last page, no credits, no signal that says you're done.
And the rewards are unpredictable, so you keep checking for the good one. "One more" is just how it works.
Also, screens. Some research suggests evening light from screens can nudge sleep later for some people.
The evidence on how big that effect is, is mixed. So I'm not saying the glow is the villain.
I'm saying it's a suspect.
So you end up somewhere strange. Exhausted, and wired. Tired, but unable to stop.
Congratulations, it's one AM, and you have zero regrets. For now.
Tomorrow Bob will have all of them.
In bulk.
Okay, enough roasting. Fixes. One for the clock, one for the "me time," and one for the finish line.
Fix one. Set an alarm for going to bed, not waking up. Thirty minutes before you want to be asleep.
It's a wind-down reminder. A homemade stopping cue, since the feed won't make one for you.
And yes, you'll swipe it away the first time.
That's fine. You noticed.
Fix two. Move some of your "me time" earlier. Even ten minutes of something just for you before dinner.
The idea is that if some of the day is already yours, the night has less to make up for.
Think of it as a deposit. A small one, before the late-night withdrawal.
Does it work for everyone? No promises. It's something to try, not a cure.
Both are free, which is the correct price for a person who can't be bothered.
And the third is my favorite, because it takes barely any discipline.
Fix three. Decide the last thing of the night before you start it. One episode. One chapter. One crossword.
The point is deciding in advance. Not "one more," in the moment, with a tired brain. The number gets set while you're awake.
Then the thing ends, the credits roll, and you get a real stopping cue. It feels illegal.
Pair it with one rule.
When the last thing finishes, the lights go out. No bonus episode.
A small honest note. If your sleep stays bad even when you do go to bed, that's worth raising with a professional.
That's it. Alarm, deposit, finish line. Three small things I can barely be bothered to say.
Remember tomorrow Bob? The one who wasn't invited, wasn't consulted, and always gets the bill?
Tonight, you could invite him.
He'll say thanks. Nobody's ever given him the chance.
